_**User (2026-03-06 09:29:41Z)**_

Build the next routing upgrade for the CSPE transport graph project without rewriting the whole app. Keep the current project structure and UI working, but improve the internal routing model so paths are more meaningful for a public transport network. The goal is to move from a simple “fewest graph jumps” model to a modular weighted routing core that can later support A*, transfer logic, agent routing, and immersive exploration.

Current state to preserve:

app/app.py already loads GTFS, builds graphs, lets the user search stops, compute a path, visualize it in 2D, and export JSON.

src/core/graph_loader.py already loads GTFS, builds cleaned edges from consecutive stops in trips, and builds NetworkX graphs by mode.

src/core/queries.py already has stop search and shortest path.

src/viz/plot2d.py already plots the network and highlighted route.
Do not break the current interface. Refactor only where needed.

Main objective:
Create a better routing layer with 2 edge families:

ride edges: normal travel edges from GTFS consecutive stops

transfer edges: artificial walking connections between nearby or same-name stops

Each edge must have richer attributes so the project can evolve later:

edge_kind: "ride" or "transfer"

mode: for ride edges, one of bus/metro/rail/tram/other; for transfer edges use "transfer"

distance_m: physical distance in meters

time_s: estimated travel time in seconds

cost: generalized routing cost used by pathfinding

keep weight_m for backward compatibility if useful, but make distance_m the new clean name internally

Architecture constraints:

Do not dump everything into app.py

Keep graph-building logic in graph_loader.py

Keep routing/pathfinding logic in queries.py

Keep export logic in tools.py

App should mostly become a caller of clean functions

Make the new design modular enough so later I can swap Dijkstra for A* or another algorithm without changing the whole app

Detailed tasks:

Refactor edge generation in src/core/graph_loader.py
Add a clearer multi-step pipeline instead of one monolithic edge build.

Create or refactor toward functions like:

build_ride_edges(...)

build_transfer_edges(...)

combine_edges(...)

build_graph(...)

Requirements for ride edges:

Continue using GTFS stop_times, trips, and routes

Two consecutive stops in a trip create one ride edge

Deduplicate undirected pairs as currently done

Preserve the mode information

Compute distance_m with haversine if coordinates are available

Estimate time_s from average speed per mode

Compute cost from time_s

Keep track of merged modes if needed in all-mode graph

Recommended default speeds:

metro: 12 m/s

rail: 16 m/s

tram: 8 m/s

bus: 5 m/s

other: 6 m/s

walking for transfers: 1.4 m/s

Important:
The exact values do not need to be perfect; they just need to create a better first routing model than raw hop count.

Add transfer edge generation
Implement transfer edges in graph_loader.py.

Goal:
Create artificial walking links between stops that a user could realistically transfer between.

Use two rules:

same-name rule: connect stops with the same normalized stop name

nearby rule: connect stops within a configurable radius in meters

Keep it conservative to avoid exploding the graph.

Recommended defaults:

same-name transfers: always allowed if coordinates exist and distance <= 400 m

nearby transfers: allowed if distance <= 200 m

do not connect a stop to itself

do not create duplicate transfer edges if a ride edge already exists between the same pair

optionally ignore transfers across very large distances even for same-name stops

Normalization for names:

lowercase

trim spaces

collapse repeated spaces

optionally remove accents only if easy, otherwise skip for now

Transfer edge attributes:

edge_kind = "transfer"

mode = "transfer"

distance_m = walking distance

time_s = distance_m / walking_speed

cost = time_s + transfer_penalty_s

Use a fixed transfer penalty so the router does not abuse transfers.
Recommended starting value:

transfer_penalty_s = 180 seconds

This penalty is important because otherwise the algorithm may prefer weird zig-zag routes with too many short transfers.

Improve graph construction
Update graph building so nodes and edges store the richer schema.

Node attributes should still include:

stop_name

lat

lon

lines if already available

Edge attributes should include at least:

edge_kind

mode or modes

distance_m

time_s

cost

optionally weight_m as alias of distance_m

For the all-mode graph:

keep enough metadata to know whether an edge is ride or transfer

if multiple ride modes collapse onto the same pair, keep a readable summary such as modes="bus|tram" or a list internally

Update the graph build entry points
Refactor build_edges_clean(...) and graph builders so the rest of the app can still call one high-level function, but internally it should now produce the richer edge set.

Recommended approach:

either replace build_edges_clean(...) with a richer version

or add a new function such as build_edges_enriched(...) and adapt app.py to use it

I would prefer a new clearer function if that makes the code cleaner.

Update pathfinding in src/core/queries.py
Refactor shortest_path(...) so it supports routing by strategy.

New behavior:

default strategy should use weighted routing on cost

optional fallback to unweighted

keep the return object simple and compatible with the current UI, but enrich it

Suggested function shape:

shortest_path(G, a, b, strategy="cost")

Supported strategies:

"cost": use cost

"distance": use distance_m

"hops": unweighted shortest path

Return object should include:

ok

reason

path

distance_m total

time_s total

transfers count if possible

maybe strategy

Implement transfer counting by counting edges where edge_kind == "transfer" along the final path.

Keep graceful fallback behavior:

missing node

disconnected graph

computation failure

Add helper utilities in queries.py
Add a function to summarize a path from edge attributes.

For example:

summarize_path(G, path)

It should compute:

total distance

total time

number of transfer edges

optionally counts by mode

This summary should be used by shortest_path(...) instead of recomputing manually.

Update app/app.py
Keep the UI mostly the same, but adapt it to the new routing model.

Changes needed:

enable enriched edge generation instead of the old compute_weights=False build

replace the old checkbox wording with something clearer

Recommended UI options:

route strategy selectbox with:

Best route (cost)

Shortest distance

Fewest stops

default should be Best route (cost)

When a path is found, display:

number of stops

estimated total distance in meters or km

estimated total time in minutes

number of transfers

Keep the existing text path download.

Do not make the UI much more complicated than it is now.

Update exports in src/core/tools.py
Improve export_graphxr(...) so exported links include the new attributes:

edge_kind

distance_m

time_s

cost

mode or modes

Improve exported nodes if easy:

include degree

keep coordinates

keep label

This will help later for immersive graph exploration.

Keep plotting compatible
plot2d.py does not need a major rewrite.
Just ensure the new graph still plots correctly.
If easy, keep path highlighting exactly as now.

Optional small improvement:
if path contains transfer edges, allow later styling differences, but do not spend much time on that now unless it is trivial.

Add validation / sanity tests
Create lightweight tests or at least internal validation functions to confirm the refactor works.

Minimum checks:

graph builds successfully for all modes

transfer edges are actually present

ride edges are still present

pathfinding works in all 3 strategies

cost-based path returns total distance and time

no crash on disconnected nodes

If there is already a test_loader.py, extend it rather than creating a messy ad hoc script.

Keep performance reasonable
The bus graph is large, so avoid an O(n²) transfer build over all stops.

Use a simple practical optimization:

same-name transfers: group by normalized name, only compare inside each group

nearby transfers: use a coarse spatial filter before exact distance checks

example: bucket by rounded lat/lon grid or only compare within nearby coordinate bins
Do not overengineer with heavy dependencies unless absolutely necessary.

If using only standard Python + pandas + NetworkX, that is preferred.

Backward-compatible coding style
Do not break current functions unless necessary.
If a cleaner new function is introduced, update the app to use it and leave comments/docstrings explaining the new preferred path.
Keep function names clear and code readable.
Do not generate giant abstractions for no reason.

Expected end result:
After the refactor, the project should still launch normally in Streamlit, but pathfinding should now be based on a realistic generalized cost model instead of just stop count. The graph should include transfer edges, and each path result should report estimated distance, time, and transfers. The codebase should be cleaner and more modular so later we can add A* routing, agent commands, and immersive interaction without rewriting everything.

Implementation priority order:

Enriched ride edges with distance_m, time_s, cost

Transfer edges

Weighted shortest path using cost

App integration

Export enrichment

Lightweight tests

Important non-goals for this step:

do not implement timetable-aware routing yet

do not implement RAPTOR yet

do not redesign the whole UI

do not add voice/agent features yet

do not try to perfectly match real-world transit times

Definition of success:

the app still works

cost-based routing is the new default

transfers are modeled

route results look more reasonable than before

the routing core is now modular enough for future upgrades

**Considering transfer edges**

I’m thinking about how transfer edges work within the same graph, especially for the user selecting metro options. Should transfers exist between metro stops and possibly nearby stops with the same name? In a mode-specific graph, transfer edges need to connect nodes relevant to that graph. If a transfer connects a metro to a bus-only node, that bus node might not be present unless it’s included through the transfer edge. I'm wondering if I should filter edges properly, maybe by including all transfers linked to the retained ride edges or just including all transfer edges.
**Developing graph structures**

I’m thinking about how to build the graph. The first step is to determine the ride edge data frame for each mode and set the allowed nodes based on the endpoints of those ride edges. Then, I should include transfer edges that have both endpoints in the allowed nodes. For the entire graph, I need to consider if a stop might have only a transfer edge with no ride edges, which may not be necessary. I also want to keep build_edges_clean as a wrapper for enriched edges since there’s the potential to use a new function, build_edges_enriched, which can work with the existing build_graphs_by_mode_with_lines function. For edge generation, I plan to merge stop times, trips, and routes, sort by trip ID and stop sequence, and create the next stop ID while ensuring rows are valid.
**Evaluating graph attributes**

If build_graph filters for mode, I can derive attributes for that requested mode from stored mode_costs when adding edges. It seems simpler to store mode_speeds in a way that isn't directly exportable. I could use a DataFrame to hold strings or dictionaries, like modes as strings and time_s_by_mode in JSON. However, aggregating distances and modes might be the way to go; when building the graph, I can recompute time and cost based on the distance and selected mode. For an all-mode graph, I’d derive from the fastest mode among the list.
**Considering update methods**

I'm thinking about updating large chunks of data. It might actually be simpler to just replace the entire file using an "apply_patch" update from the top instead of dealing with smaller parts. This way, I can ensure everything gets updated consistently and minimize potential issues. It feels like a more straightforward approach! Let’s go with that method for a smoother process.
**Considering similar names and records**

I’m thinking that for entries with the same name, I should probably use a radius of 400. When dealing with a group of the same name, I can call on their group records. If the group is small, the same helper should work fine. For nearby records across all stops, I might need to call a helper with the nearby radius. This could connect the same names as well, but I’ve noticed that deduplication handles that. It might be worth combining edges just by concatenating and sorting by edge kind.</details></think>

_**Agent (gpt-5.4-medium)**_

Implemented the routing upgrade without changing the app’s overall structure or UI flow.

## What Changed
`src/core/graph_loader.py` now has a modular enriched pipeline:
- `build_ride_edges(...)` builds GTFS consecutive-stop ride edges with `edge_kind`, `mode`/`modes`, `distance_m`, `time_s`, `cost`, and `weight_m`.
- `build_transfer_edges(...)` adds conservative walking transfers using same-name and nearby-stop rules, with walking time plus a fixed transfer penalty.
- `combine_edges(...)` and `build_edges_enriched(...)` provide the new high-level entry point.
- Existing `build_edges_clean(...)` still exists as a compatibility wrapper.

`src/core/queries.py` now supports strategy-based routing:
- `shortest_path(G, a, b, strategy="cost")`
- Strategies: `cost`, `distance`, `hops`
- Added `summarize_path(...)` so results include `distance_m`, `time_s`, `transfers`, and mode counts.

`app/app.py` now uses the enriched graph build and exposes a route strategy selector:
- `Best route (cost)` is the default
- `Shortest distance`
- `Fewest stops`

Path results now show stop count, estimated distance, estimated time, and transfers. `src/core/tools.py` exports richer node/link metadata for GraphXR, including `edge_kind`, `distance_m`, `time_s`, `cost`, `mode`/`modes`, and node degree.

## Validation
Extended `src/test_loader.py` into a lightweight validation script and ran it successfully with:

```text
python src/test_loader.py
```

It verified:
- graph builds for all modes
- ride and transfer edges both exist
- routing works for `cost`, `distance`, and `hops`
- cost routing reports distance and time
- missing/disconnected cases fail gracefully

I did not launch the Streamlit UI interactively here, but the underlying graph build, routing, and export paths are all passing the validation script. A natural next step would be a small visual pass in the app to confirm the new route summaries feel right for a few real stop pairs.

_**Agent (gpt-5.4-medium)**_

The failure was caused by Streamlit caching, not by the routing math. `build_graphs(...)` was decorated with `@st.cache_resource`, but Streamlit still tried to hash its huge `GTFSData` and `DataFrame` arguments, which triggered the `deepcopy`/`ArrayMemoryError`.

I fixed `app/app.py` so:
- `load_all(...)` now uses `@st.cache_resource` instead of `@st.cache_data`
- `build_graphs(...)` keeps `@st.cache_resource`, but its parameters are renamed to `_data`, `_edges_clean`, `_pos_all`, which makes Streamlit skip hashing those large objects

That should stop the mid-test memory blowups while preserving the current app behavior.

If Streamlit still has the bad cached state in memory, restart the app once or clear Streamlit’s cache and rerun. If you want, I can also make one more pass to reduce baseline memory usage in the enriched edge table itself.

path = optional list of nodes representing a route

3D graph layout

x = longitude
y = latitude
z = node importance

degree = G.degree(node)

Use Plotly inside Streamlit:

st.plotly_chart(fig, use_container_width=True)

If the graph has more than 5000 nodes:

the route

neighbors within 2 hops

view highlighted routes

_**Agent (gpt-5.4-medium)**_

Added a separate 3D visualization layer without changing the routing or export core.

`src/viz/plot3d.py` now provides `plot_graph_3d(G, pos, path=None)` using Plotly. It places nodes at longitude/latitude, lifts them by degree-based importance, sizes them by connectivity, colors transfers separately from ride edges, and highlights the selected route in red. For large graphs, it automatically narrows the view to a route-centered 2-hop subgraph so Plotly stays usable.

`app/app.py` now has a `Visualization mode` selector in the existing right-hand panel:
- `2D map`
- `3D network`

The 2D view is unchanged. When `3D network` is selected, the app renders the Plotly figure with `st.plotly_chart(...)`, and if the graph is large it shows a small caption explaining that the 3D view is focused for responsiveness.

I also added `plotly==6.4.0` to `requirements.txt` and installed it into the project `.venv`, then verified the new module imports correctly in that environment.

If you want, the next small upgrade could be adding a legend or toggle for node coloring by mode vs by degree.
